what_the_class_is: The section a filter byte's corner sits on, as opposed to where the corner is. A byte that names a frequency and has no gain beside it is a filter that cuts past its corner rather than a shelf that tilts the two sides against each other, and how steeply it cuts is how many poles it is made of. The frequency class settled which corners a byte reaches and left this untouched: one reading says where the curve sits and the other says what the curve is.

era.when: Mid nineteen-nineties, a custom fixed-point DSP running its effects at a rate below the converter's, with a stored coefficient set per table entry.
what_that_implies: A pole costs one coefficient and a pair costs two, so a table of sixteen corners is sixteen numbers for one pole and thirty-two for a pair. The frequency class already leans on that arithmetic to argue a table of sixteen is affordable and a table of a hundred and twenty-eight of them is not, so what the entry holds is the thing that argument was made about.

A section is written once and reached by more than one byte. A part that has a one-pole low pass has a one-pole high pass, because the two are the same difference equation with the numerator changed, and giving one of them a second pole would be a second routine to write and a second coefficient to store.

The rate the effect runs at is not the converter's, and a low pass is where that shows. The bilinear transform leaves a zero at half the rate, so the skirt bends steeper as it climbs towards it -- a section running at six decibels an octave in the middle of the band and at ten near the top has named where half the rate is. Nothing in a high pass does: its zero is at nothing, and where the warp would show is its own flat passband.
era.would_be_wrong_if: The skirt ran at a slope no whole number of poles gives, or the same byte's low and high settings returned corners that did not agree, or a low pass's skirt stayed at six decibels an octave all the way to the top of the band -- which would put half the rate well outside it.

candidates.reading: One pole a filter, at the rate two other classes on this unit have named independently.
candidates.predicts: Six decibels an octave through the middle of the band, bending to about ten by 12.7 kHz as the low pass approaches its zero at 16 kHz, and three decibels down at the corner.

candidates.reading: The same section clocked at the converter's rate rather than the part's.
candidates.predicts: The same six decibels an octave, and no bend worth reading anywhere the band set reaches -- half of 44.1 kHz is above the top band.

candidates.reading: The same section at the other rate of the era's converters.
candidates.predicts: The same again, with the bend further off still.

candidates.reading: Two identical poles cascaded rather than one.
candidates.predicts: Twelve decibels an octave on the skirt and six down at the corner.

candidates.reading: A conjugate pole pair at the flattest resonance, which is the biquad a part with biquads would reach for.
candidates.predicts: The same twelve decibels an octave far from the corner and three decibels down at it, so it is told from the cascade there and not on the skirt.
